t: LeetCode 2065 - Maximum Path Quality of a Graph: Constraint-Bounded Backtracking
o: **Understanding the problem.** Among all walks that start and end at node 0 and take at most maxTime seconds (edges reusable, nodes revisitable), maximize the sum of values of the distinct nodes touched - each node pays out at most once. Example 1: the tour 0 -> 1 -> 0 -> 3 -> 0 spends 10+10+10+10 = 40 seconds, within the budget of 49, and collects 0+32+43 = 75. Example 3 allows 0 -> 1 -> 3 -> 1 -> 0 at cost 46, collecting 1+2+4 = 7 - note how node 1 is crossed twice but counted once. The decisive hints hide in the constraints: every edge costs at least 10 while maxTime is at most 100, so a walk has at most ten edges, and with at most four edges per node the search space is on the order of a few million walks - tiny. Exhaustive DFS with backtracking is therefore the intended solution, not a naive fallback.
k: maxTime divided by the minimum edge time bounds any walk to at most 10 edges regardless of n = 1000.
Degree at most 4 caps the branching factor, making exhaustive backtracking provably cheap.
A node value is banked only on its first visit; afterwards the node may still be crossed for free as a corridor.
Quality can reach about 10^11 (values up to 10^8), so accumulate in 64 bits.

a.i: Launch a DFS from node 0 holding elapsed time, accumulated quality, and a visited flag per node. Every in-budget edge may be taken; entering a node for the first time banks its value and sets its flag, undone on backtrack. Standing on node 0 updates the best answer, and already-visited nodes serve as free passages.
s: Build the adjacency list; start the DFS at 0 with time 0 and quality values[0], marking 0 visited.
Whenever the DFS stands on node 0, update the global best.
Discard any move whose accumulated time exceeds maxTime.
Take each surviving edge: mark unvisited neighbors, add their value once, recurse, then restore the flag.
Already-visited neighbors are traversed with zero additional value.
a.t: O(4^d) with d at most maxTime/10 = 10 - branching bounded by degree 4, depth bounded by the edge budget
a.sp: O(n) - adjacency list, visited array, and recursion depth of at most 11

a.n: Approach 2: Prune With Shortest Return Distance
a.i: Precompute dist[v] as the shortest travel time from v to 0 with one Dijkstra from node 0 over the undirected graph. During the DFS skip any move for which spent time plus edge cost plus dist[next] already exceeds maxTime - such walks could never close. Pruned branches provably contain no completed valid walk, so correctness holds while the tree shrinks.
s: Run Dijkstra from node 0 to fill the distance array.
Repeat the Approach 1 DFS with one extra cutoff: require time + t + dist[next] <= maxTime.
Value banking, backtracking, and recording at 0 stay unchanged.
a.t: O(n^2 + 4^d) - an O(V^2) Dijkstra adds negligible preprocessing and pruning only removes branches
a.sp: O(n) - distance array beside the existing structures

w: Sell the constraint analysis first: at most ten edges and four-way branching is exactly what legitimizes brute force - reaching for heavy machinery wastes the interview. Pitfalls: forbidding passage through already-visited nodes (example 3 needs node 1 twice), forgetting that the starting node contributes values[0], and overflowing 32-bit sums. Follow-ups: if maxTime were large the argument collapses and you would need meet-in-the-middle or DP over visited sets; if values paid per visit the structure changes entirely.
